data.section: Gaps

title: india_toolkit_redflags › Gaps

body:
- The verifiable money in the Sundar story is advisory and education revenue: about ₹4.6 crore in fees in roughly 2020–2022 from Telegram calls alone, before workshops and YouTube. His trading P&L is entirely self-reported, and no audited track record exists. Retail investors should treat claimed option-selling returns as unverified marketing.
- Short options (short straddles and strangles) have negative skew: frequent small gains and rare large losses, such as gap moves in March 2020, election-result days or budget days. His own "lost ₹15 lakh in a day" tweet shows the intraday tail even for a well-capitalised trader. Retail sellers with smaller capital and margins are more exposed to forced exits at the worst prices.
- SEBI's study did not break out option sellers in any source I found, so whether option sellers do better than buyers among individuals is unverified. The broad result (about 91% lose, with prop/algo desks taking the profits) suggests that copying a famous seller's style is not a reliable retail edge.

  same bias.

title: lessons › L15 (2026-11-21) — Historical blind drills don't work for an LLM; forward calls are the test

body:
| step | D (census) | X (sample of BSE/NSE delisted) | L (sample of live) |
|---|---|---|---|
| companies sampled (weight) | 1,739 (1.0) | 500 (4.264) | 900 (5.633) |
| no screener page | 795 | 213 | 14 |
| financial (excluded) | 57 | 8 + 6 unlabeled banks | 107 |
| rows FY2016: no annual data at T / no price history / not trading at T / size unknown / outside ₹200–20,000 cr | 236 / 36 / 141 / 55 / 313 | 210 / 23 / 21 / 1 / 14 | 201 / 8 / 133 / 27 / 265 |
| rows FY2018: same | 333 / 31 / 132 / 50 / 264 | 240 / 12 / 13 / 0 / 7 | 177 / 9 / 116 / 39 / 276 |
| already in insolvency at T (excluded) | 6 (FY2018) | 0 | 0 |
| **panel rows** FY2016 + FY2018 | **106 + 71 = 177** | **4 + 1 = 5** | **145 + 162 = 307** |

Panel: **489 company-snapshots** (FY2016 255, FY2018 234). Outcomes in the panel: O_liq 19, O_cdel 29, O_px 165,
**O_fail 168** (weighted base rate **19.7%**: FY2016 27.6%, FY2018 12.2%), O_strict 33 (1.7%), O_cirp admissions 79,
winners ≥ 3x 92. "Not trading at T" among live names is mostly companies that listed after T (IPOs from 2017–2023
whose earlier annual data screener holds). 20 rows have an ambiguous size (rounding interval straddles a boundary).

**Survivorship audit (retrievability of the dead lists):**

| list | companies in frame | screener page | annual data at a T | in panel |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| IBBI liquidation | 169 | 144 (85%) | 115 | 22 |
| IBBI CIRP admission | 492 | 409 (83%) | 350 | 85 |
| NSE compulsory / liquidation delisting | 204 | 203 (100%) | 65 | 5 |
| BSE suspended | 1,213 | 494 (41%) | 446 | 55 |
| NSE suspended (pre-2012) | 128 | 121 | 47 | 0 |
| IBBI rows with no exchange identifier | 221 | not fetchable | – | – |

The IBBI dead firms are 83–85% retrievable. The missing 15–17% are mostly renamed or merged companies; together with
the 221 IBBI rows that had no identifier, this leak means *fewer* failures in the panel. BSE-suspended companies
without a page are mostly old shells far below ₹200 cr. Most NSE compulsory delistings had stopped filing before T,
so they were not live filers. Stratum D has a 68.9% weighted O_fail rate and stratum L 14.7%: dead companies do get
in, and the panel is not a survivors-only set. Price coverage: R5 is missing for 50 rows (the series stopped early);
winner status is unknown for 9.

These come in this order: thesis in one line → variant view → what the price implies (stage 5) → stage 2 hard filters and graded
flags → stage 3 signals (PEAD avoid flag, sector-adjusted credibility, detector alerts) → stage 4 soft flags and
the override log → P(≥3x/5y), P(≤0.5x), P(blow-up) next to their base rates → expected value → position size by
the written rule → dated kill criteria → pre-mortem → gate log and review date.

title: lessons › L15 (2026-11-21) — Historical blind drills don't work for an LLM; forward calls are the test

body:
Two safeguards from the 2026-11-23 back-tests. Neither changes the hurdle or any v1.1 gate threshold.

**1. Survival cap, India only (L35, `decision:pead-avoid-plus-redflag-survival-cap`).** It fires when the PEAD avoid flag
is active (bottom-two SUE quintile within ~63 trading days) **and** either promoter pledge is above 25% of the
promoter holding or interest cover is below 1.5x. Input: card field `survival` with `pledge_pct_of_promoter` (fraction),
`interest_cover` (x), `already_owned`, `source`, `as_of` and `note`. If the window is active and an input is missing,
the status is UNCHECKED and the cap is treated as triggered until the input is checked, as a stage-2 `unknown` would be.
- **Policy chosen: 0 new money, not a minimum size.** If the stock is already owned, the position goes to
  **hold-review**: no additions, and it is reviewed against the balance-sheet question. The red flag is a solvency
  risk, and a small new position would still be money committed to a ~3x halving risk (17.6% vs 6.1% in 12 months).
- The card prints a **mandatory balance-sheet question** (debt service and the promoter's ability to meet a margin
  call through a 12-month stress, answered from filings rather than from management) and logs the gate as blocking.
- **S5-India alone is not a trigger** (no signal in the test). Outside the window, and in the US, the cap is `n/a`.
- While the window is open, the PEAD WAIT gate already sets the size to 0. What the cap adds is the hold-review rule
  for existing holders, the balance-sheet question, and a separate gate-log entry. That entry shows *why* the WAIT is
  a survival issue and not just drift.
